newsitem.title: UK: ALLIANCE & LEICESTER NOT EXPECTED TO SURPRISE.
newsitem.headline: ALLIANCE & LEICESTER NOT EXPECTED TO SURPRISE.

text.p: British building society-turned-bank Alliance & Leicester will report its first set of results as a publicly listed company next Friday, with analysts keen to know if it has seen an outflow of business since conversion in April.

Analysts on Friday predicted pre-tax profits, before Alliance & Leicester's exceptional costs associated with conversion and flotation of 32 million stg, of between 179 million stg and 194 million stg.
An Alliance & Leicester spokesman told Reuters it spent 26 million stg in 1996 of the 58 million stg it had assigned for the costs of conversion.
Most analysts said Alliance & Leicester would pay its new shareholders an interim dividend of 6.0p per share, although one suggested 6.7p.
But few expect any surprises from the bank, which has been joined by other building societies in ditching its mutual status.

"No surprises are expected from Alliance & Leicester for the first half of 1997, as the business continues to follow the strategy outlined prior to demutualisation," Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said in a recent research note.
Morgan Stanley expected the bank to have a prominent position in the mortgage market for the first half, with net lending likely to be above its natural share of around four percent.
While mortgage discounts and cashbacks are no less important in winning new business, pricing pressure had eased slightly, it added.
But Goldman Sachs said the bank's mortgage business was "still inefficient" and cost cutting could be achieved, making the shares more attractive.

Analysts were keen to find out how successful the first of the current wave of demutualising building societies to float was in keeping the money which members poured into it to ensure maximum "windfall" share payout.

Depositors may have chosen to spend money they had used to "top up" accounts, while so-called "carpetbaggers" could shift cash to remaining building societies as they speculate on which will next demutualise.
Some savers may chase higher rates of return at other firms or change their investment class.

One analysts said there had been sufficient time for the effects to begin to show, although Morgan Stanley said the shift would be in line with management expectations but would edge down Alliance & Leicester's net interest margin.
The second analyst said the focus would be on Alliance & Leicester's cost ratio, with anticipation raised after Woolwich's success in bringing down costs, which it reported earlier this week.
Morgan Stanley said it expects costs "to show modest absolute growth but hold flat in real terms". Branch numbers will edge lower and staff numbers fall to a target range of 8,400-8,500, it added.
Alliance & Leicester's Girobank operation, which deals with money transfer and commercial banking, is expected to be under pressure, with flat profits.
But the bank's unsecured lending, including credit cards, is expected to perform well.
Forecasts for Alliance & Leicester's 1997 performance range from pre-tax profits of 329-343 million stg.
But most analysts thought the bank's shares, which had fallen 7.0p to 610p by 1125 GMT, were still overpriced, with targets of 527-560 pence.
Speculation of a buy-back or possible acquisitions was unlikely to die down, analysts said. Alliance & Leicester is estimated by some to have excess capital of around 600 million stg.
It is also seen as a takeover target, despite in-built defence from legislation protecting former building societies.
